Programmable photonic integrated circuits can realize analog matrix multiplication to accelerate
computing disruptively in various ﬁelds. However, a major challenge is the precise voltage
conﬁguration of the circuit to deal with the universal static error derived from manufacturing. Here, we
propose a complete off-chip method based on the combination of gradient descent and genetic
algorithms to ﬁnd the optimal conﬁguration for an arbitrary matrix, enabling imperfect circuits to
achieve excellent performance. In the simulation, we demonstrated that our method implements an
arbitrary matrix with an average ﬁdelity of 0.992 on a Mach–Zehnder-interferometer-based circuit with
up to 28 input ports. Experimentally, we demonstrated superior performance on the circuit with 4 input
ports, including training a theoretical model that characterized the experimental imperfections of the
fabricated chip and obtaining the optimal conﬁguration for permutation matrices with near-one ﬁdelity
and for 100 unitary matrices with a 0.985 average ﬁdelity.
Programmablephotonicintegrated circuits(PPICs),whichareanalogousto
the ﬁeld-programmable gate array in optical domain1–3, integrate optical
devices, such as waveguides, couplers, beam splitters, Mach–Zehnder
interferometers (MZIs), microring resonators, and photodetectors, onto
silicon-based chips. These components enable precise manipulation of the
optical signal ﬂow within the chip via external electrical signal interfaces.
The rapid advancement of CMOS-compatible fabrication processes in
recent years has propelled research on PPICs for analog optical computing
into a prominent frontier. Meanwhile, PPICs exhibit ultra-high bandwidth,
massively parallel signal processing capabilities with multiple degrees of
freedom, and low power consumption attributed to near-zero energy con-
sumption during light propagation, establishing them as a rapidly evolving
photonic technology. Nowadays, PPICs are introduced into various ﬁelds,
such as quantum computing4, multifunctional ﬁlters5,6, optical neural
networks7–10, and optical computing11–14.
However, the major challenge facing the application of PPICs is the
precise control of the circuits to achieve excellent performance3. Due to the
wavelength-sensitive nature of optical components, the fabrication toler-
ances of devices in PPICsare typically constrained to the nanometer scale.It
is challenging for current manufacturing technologies to ensure that the
dimensions of fabricated devices precisely match design speciﬁcations.
These imperfect devices in PPICs cause uncertain performances and, in
most cases, signiﬁcant deviations from designed functions. For example, an
experimental angled multimode interference, with an insertion loss of
3.3 dB and a channel nonuniformity of 1.28 dB, was observed to be higher
than the simulated values of 2.36 dB and 0.86 dB, respectively15. Further-
more, the experimental vowel classiﬁcation accuracy of an MZI-based
optical neural network was reduced by 15% compared with the simulation
result7.
To address the above challenges, several methods, categorized into
on-chip and off-chip methods, each with distinct advantages, have been
reported16–19. We previously proposed an on-chip training method for
optical neural networks using a neuroevolution algorithm to avoid the
inﬂuence of manufacturing errors20. Similar ideas have been constantly
reported, including numerical optimization algorithms and other
heuristic algorithms21–24. However, running an algorithm once for a
speciﬁc task causes run times to grow rapidly when circuit complexity
increases. Similarly, as with on-chip single-objective optimization
algorithms, gradient-based methods derive optimization paths by in-
situ computing25 or by estimating gradients26, making them particularly
effective for large-scale photonic circuits with complex architectures.
Moreover, there are additional on-chip optimization algorithms that, by
leveraging techniques such as speciﬁc topological structures27, system
symmetries28, and frequency response relationships29, have demon-
strated effective performance in optical neural networks, optical ﬁlters,
and other applications. However, the on-chip approach relies on

new target application. In contrast, through technologies implemented
outside the chip, off-chip methods enable the parallel provision of vol-
tage conﬁgurations required for multiple target transmission matrices or
speciﬁc tasks. Based on circuit parameter measurements, the phase shift
values of phase shifters are systematically adjusted to compensate for the
imbalance of adjacent couplers30. However, this method is only designed
to compensate for the error of couplers, and the compensation range is
limited. The transmission matrices of imperfect devices, often regarded
as black boxes, are trained using gradient descent algorithms to ﬁnd
numerical models of PPICs31. Tandem neural networks are built to
rapidly predict phase conﬁgurations for PPICs32. However, the methods
that treat transmission matrices as black-box models are difﬁcult to scale
on high-dimensional and complicated circuits. Clear-box methods
based on gradient descent algorithms are implemented to train
numerical models of PPICs using the PyTorch package in Python33,
enabling the search for voltage conﬁgurations of target applications.
However, real-time experimental measurements are introduced during
algorithms to escape multiple local optimal solutions, resulting in long
run times and reduced method ﬂexibilities. Similar studies based on
gradient descent algorithms have been reported to build numerical
models for obtaining optimized phase conﬁgurations34–36.
In this paper, we propose an efﬁcient and completely off-chip method
that combines gradient descent algorithms and genetic algorithms, enabling
imperfect PPICs to achieve excellent performance. Our proposed method
outperforms previous approaches in several key aspects: (1) It is a com-
pletely off-chip algorithm that avoids the disturbance caused by experi-
mental measurements during training and further reduces the time
consumption of the algorithm. (2) It introduces a genetic algorithm that
signiﬁcantly decreases the difﬁculty of training a theoretical model and has
the potential to be extended to large-scale circuits. (3) It fully accounts for
various sources of error and can be ﬂexibly adjusted according to the actual
experimental setup, making the found conﬁguration achieve excellent
experimental performance. (4) It provides a universal idea for effective
conﬁguration. The method is not only suitable for typical designs but also
useful for other custom designs, and can even be extended to circuits
composed of other devices.
Method
Theoretical model for imperfect PPICs
As shown in Fig. 1, the typical N × N physical implementation of PPIC is
composed of N × (N-1)/2 MZIs and N extra phase shifters, which is
effective as a weight matrix. Each programmable MZI consists of two
3-dB directional couplers, an internal phase shifter (θ), and an external
phase shifter (φ)37. The phase shift value of each extra phase shifter is
marked as δ. The input signal X is a complex value characterized by
amplitude and phase. The process by which signal X passes through the
circuit can be regarded as a matrix-vector multiplication operation.
Theoretically, a circuit transmission matrix can realize an arbitrary
unitary operator by setting the phase shifters to a corresponding phase
value. In the ideal case, regardless of the static errors occasioned by
imperfect fabrications and the dynamic errors brought on by the noises
induced from the devices used, such as phase shifters, modulators, and
photodetectors, and redundant waveguides designed to ensure the
symmetry of circuits, the conﬁguration of phase shifters required for an
arbitrary unitary operator can be calculated by decomposition
algorithm38. In effect, it is inevitable for the performance of the manu-
factured device to be inconsistent with its design. In summary, the
transmission matrix of an MZI with error can be expressed as follows:

AlthoughtheAdamalgorithmcanquicklyﬁndtheoptimalsolution,its
search is easily affected by the initial value of the population. In other words,
Adam algorithms achieve localoptimal solutions with increasing modelsize
and the complexity of deﬁned error parameters. To further enhance the

population enters the next round of the Adam algorithm for gradient

Clearly, the gradient descent algorithm was seriously affected by the initial

individuals in the ﬁrst round of gradient descent trapped into the local

Thus, by introducing the genetic algorithm, our proposed conﬁguration
method effectively made up for the disadvantage of the gradient descent

Experimental setup
The experimental demonstration presented in this work built a theoretical
model with imperfections for an N = 4 PPIC and found the optimal phase
conﬁguration for various permutation matrices to validate the effectiveness
of the theoretical model. The experimental setup is depicted in Fig. 4a. A
polarization-maintaining continuous tuning laser operates at 1550 nm with
up to 15.5 dBm optical power (ID Photonics CoBrite-DX4). A polarization-
maintaining isolator was connected after the laser was used to ensure the
one-way propagation of the circuit. The chip of PPIC, designed following
Reck’s proposal43, was manufactured on a 220 nm silicon-on-insulator
substrate using a 180 nm lithography node. The details of our fabricated
integrated circuit are shown in the right panel of Fig. 4a. The polarization-
maintaining ﬁber array was adapted to vertically couple with the grating
coupler array of the chip. A Thermo-Electric Cooler was employed to sta-
bilize the chip temperature at 25 ± 0.01 °C to minimize the inﬂuence of

Experimental result
Following the step depicted in Fig. 2, we ﬁrst built the theoretical model for
the imperfect PPIC according to the experimental optical circuit design and
initialized a population Ω with nind = 10. Next, we established the rela-
tionshipbetweentheappliedvoltagevalueandtheexperimentalphasevalue
for each phase shifter. Traversing the voltage of 900 points from 0 V to 9 V,

Conclusion
In summary, we proposed a ﬁve-step off-chip training method to determine
the optimal conﬁguration for an arbitrary matrix in an experimental PPIC.
First, through extensive simulations, we theoretically demonstrated the
feasibility of our method in dealing with the typical set of static errors in the
case of N = 4, 8, 16, 24, and 28, respectively. Furthermore, by introducing
extra dynamic noise to the phase shifter of the simulated model, we show
that our method can still ﬁnd the optimal conﬁguration for an arbitrary
matrix with high ﬁdelity, demonstrating the robustness of our proposed
method. Ultimately, by building a complete experimental platform of
optical analog computing based on an N = 4 PPIC, we experimentally
demonstrated the feasibility and superior performance of the method,
including training a theoretical model that characterized the experimental
imperfections, and obtaining the optimal conﬁguration for various per-
mutationmatrices withnear-oneﬁdelityand for100unitarymatriceswith a
0.985 average ﬁdelity. As shown in Table 1, we propose a complete off-chip
method that comprehensivelyconsiders varioussourcesof errorand hasthe
potential to be applied to large-scale circuits. In our future work, we will
enhance computational parallelism by recompiling the Python code into a
more efﬁcient language, thereby exploring the performance of our method
on large-scale circuits.
